candidates.title: The soaring cost of shipping is lifting the price of oil for consumers - IEA
candidates.source_name: The soaring cost of shipping is lifting the price of oil for consumers - IEA
candidates.snippet:
The effects are spreading across the global tanker market
As vessels spend longer on disrupted routes, demand has spilled over into smaller tankers. Instead of using VLCCs, charterers have been splitting crude cargoes across smaller Suezmax and Aframax vessels, driving up demand for both.
In the third quarter of 2026, demand for these two tanker classes, measured on a tonne-mile basis – which accounts for both the volume of cargo transported and the distance it travels – was around 20% higher than a year earlier.
By mid-October, shipping crude from West Africa to Europe on a Suezmax vessel cost over $22 per barrel, more than four times pre-conflict levels. North Sea Aframax rates also tripled, reaching over $6 per barrel.
The impact has extended into the product tanker market.
As a result, oil product cargoes have been redistributed across the fleet of smaller vessels, tightening shipping capacity throughout the product tanker market. Freight rates for Long Range 1 (LR1) tankers travelling from the Middle East Gulf to Japan were nearly $27 per barrel in mid-October, five times higher than before the conflict.
Further disruptions to global oil trade could tighten tanker markets even more. The prospect of a US diesel export ban added to concerns of further trade dislocation in September. Such a measure would have reduced demand for tankers in the Atlantic Basin but increased the need for longer-distance shipments from Asia to Europe and Latin America.

candidates.source_name: The Middle East and Global Energy Markets – Topics - IEA
candidates.snippet:
Through ship-to-ship transfers and alternative export routes to the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil exports from Gulf producers surged to 13.9 million barrels per day in September, reaching over 75% of pre-war levels, according to our latest Oil Market Report .
In 2025, Gulf producers exported 3.3 million barrels per day of refined oil products and 1.5 million barrels per day of liquefied petroleum gas. Nearly 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity in the region remains shut due to attacks and a lack of viable export outlets.
Global oil demand is now expected to fall by 2.6 million barrels per day on average in 2026.
With buffers shrinking and the global refining system stretched to the limit, the report emphasises that the need for progress in resolving the conflict in the Middle East is greater than ever to avoid further market tightening and demand destruction.
IEA’s role and oil stock release
On 11 March, IEA Member countries unanimously agreed to take emergency collective action to respond to the major disruptions in oil markets, making 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks available – the largest-ever release coordinated by the Agency.
Why is the Strait of Hormuz so important?
Only Saudi Arabia and the UAE have operational crude pipelines that could potentially reroute flows to bypass the Strait, with an estimated 3.5 million barrels per day to 5.5 million barrels per day of available capacity.

Why a third benchmark exists
Brent and WTI are light, sweet crudes: low density, low sulfur. The barrels that dominate eastbound Gulf exports are medium gravity and sour - higher sulfur, requiring different refinery configurations. A light sweet benchmark misprices them, particularly when the light-heavy spread moves.
A narrowing Brent-Dubai spread makes Atlantic-basin crude competitive in Asia and typically accompanies strength in sour grades or weakness in sweet; a widening spread pushes Asian buyers back toward Gulf barrels.

In 2014, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) began to send its crude oil to the world market via Turkey’s Ceyhan port and the Iraq-Turkish pipeline, despite Baghdad’s protests. Seven years later, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a ruling on March 25 that this trade was a violation of the 1973 agreement.
Turkey’s response to the ICC ruling was immediate; it informed Iraq that Ankara would no longer allow KRG crude oil to be loaded onto ships at Ceyhan port without permission from Baghdad.
In response, oil firms operating in the Kurdistan Region stopped production or reduced output, diverting their remaining output into already mostly-full storage.
For its part, Baghdad has rejected KRG oil trade to Turkey from the beginning, sparking the initial ICC case. At that time, former Iraqi Oil minister Hussian Shehrstani said, “any oil exportation should be via the federally-owned State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) and any step outside of SOMO is illegal.”
During his term as Iraqi Prime minister, Haidar al-Abadi likewise asked the KRG to export 250,000 bpd via SOMO, but KRG again refused. Then, Mustafa al-Kadhimi increased the rate to 400,000 bpd via SOMO, but KRG refused all of the requests, and has been exporting the oil through its pipelines instead.
This represents a major concession for the KRG and a shift in the relations between the two entities, and has been a request from previous governments in Baghdad for years.

LONDON: Five vessels loaded with liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Ras Laffan, Qatar, are approaching the Strait of Hormuz, ship-tracking data showed on Saturday.
If the vessels successfully crossed the strait, it would be the first transit of LNG cargoes through the waterway since the US-Israel war with Iran began on February 28.
On Friday, Iran reopened the strait, which before the war carried a fifth of the world’s LNG trade, following a separate US-brokered ceasefire agreement on Thursday by Israel and Lebanon. A convoy of oil tankers was crossing the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday.
“Currently we see five laden vessels approaching the Strait of Hormuz. All five vessels loaded from Qatar’s Ras Laffan plant. Of the five, two are destined for Pakistan, two likely destined for India and one with no clear destination,” said Laura Page, manager of LNG Insight at Kpler.
“In addition, two ballast Adnoc vessels enter the Gulf of Oman and moor outside Fujairah. The vessel movements align with flaring data which suggests multiple trains at Ras Laffan’s north site have restarted as well as UAE’s Das Island plant,” she added.
Qatar is the world’s second-largest exporter of LNG, with shipments mostly going to buyers in Asia. Iranian attacks, however, knocked out 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG export capacity, with repairs expected to sideline 12.8 million metric tonnes per year of the fuel for three to five years.

The 48-hour ultimatum issued by the Trump administration regarding the Strait of Hormuz represents a classic application of Strategic Compellence —the use of threats to persuade an adversary to undo an action already taken or to initiate a specific behavior.

The Mechanics of the Hormuz Choke Point
The most significant threat to the 48-hour deadline is not a direct naval engagement, but the deployment of sea mines. Modern bottom-moored mines are difficult to detect and can be deployed rapidly by non-military vessels.
The physics of de-mining is a slow, methodical process.
Even with advanced Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) and Mk 18 Mod 2 Kingfish systems, clearing a 21-mile wide strait takes weeks, not hours.
Therefore, the "48-hour deadline" is less about clearing the water and more about establishing Escalation Dominance —convincing the adversary that the cost of laying mines will be the total destruction of their naval and economic infrastructure.

“But there may not be sufficient consensus in the policy board for successive rate hikes given the fragility in the domestic bond market,” he added.

The Army introduced the program in 2025 after an executive order called for the military to speed up its integration of nuclear power, with the goal of having an operational reactor at a military base by Sept. 30, 2028.

None of the base’s future reactors use highly enriched — or weapon’s grade — uranium, according to Jeff Waksman, principal deputy assistant secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment.
